title: What AI does better than most lawyers, and what it cannot do
summary: AI tools are now strong at reading, organising and drafting legal material on paper, and they can make a prepared person much more capable. They cannot verify the real world, carry responsibility or sign for you, and that line decides how you should use them.
body:
Bottom line. AI is a strong reader, organiser and first drafter. It is not a person who can be held responsible. Use it to do the work that sits on paper, and keep for yourself and your professionals the work that needs judgment about the real world and a signature that someone must answer for.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, in 2026 a university lecturer named Greg Baker represented himself at Australia's Fair Work Commission, the national workplace tribunal, using AI tools to prepare his case. As reported, he won. On the podcast that introduced this course, Baker says AI is already better than most humans at legal reasoning on paper, and that written submissions favour AI. That is his opinion, and the university was reported to be considering an appeal. But the case shows something real: where the facts and the rules are both in writing, a prepared person with good tools can do far more than before.

The same story also shows the limit. Baker, not the software, stood in front of the tribunal. He answered for every word filed. AI can help you think. It cannot be the one who is responsible.

In this lesson, AI means a large language model, a program trained on very large amounts of text that can read your documents and produce new text in reply. ChatGPT and Claude are examples.

The framework

Sort every task into one of two lists.

What AI often does better or faster than a busy human professional:

  • Reading volume. It can read a 60-page lease in seconds and list every date, payment and consent requirement.
  • Consistency checks. It can compare a definition against every clause that uses it, which tired people miss.
  • Structure. It can turn a messy timeline of emails into an ordered chronology, and an argument into an IRAC outline.
  • First drafts. It can produce a clear first draft of a letter, a summary or a list of questions.
  • The other side's view. It can argue against your position on request, without getting tired or defensive.

What AI cannot do:

  • Carry responsibility. It cannot sign, cannot be disciplined, holds no licence and has no insurance. The person who files or signs answers for the content.
  • Verify the real world. It cannot see the land, read today's land register, or know what was said in a meeting it was not told about.
  • Guarantee the law is current or real. It can describe a rule that has changed, or invent a case that does not exist. The next lesson covers this.
  • Judge people. It cannot read a counterparty's mood or decide how hard to push a lender you need again next year.
  • Protect confidentiality by itself. What you paste into a tool may be stored or reviewed under that tool's terms. Communications with a lawyer may be protected by privilege, which is a legal protection that keeps them confidential; communications with an AI tool generally are not [confirm independently with counsel].

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer receives a 60-page commercial lease from a tenant's lawyer for a 5,000-square-foot unit at 25 per square foot per year, which is 125,000 a year. A lawyer's full review might take four hours at 500 per hour, which is 2,000.

The developer first asks an AI tool to list every date, every payment, every clause needing landlord consent, and every place the lease differs from the developer's standard form. The tool produces a two-page table in minutes. It flags that the tenant has a right to terminate after year two, which the developer had missed.

The developer then sends the table and the lease to counsel, with three specific questions. The lawyer spends one and a half hours instead of four, which is about 750 instead of 2,000, and spends that time on judgment: is the termination right enforceable, and what should it cost the tenant?

What the AI could not do: confirm the tenant's company exists, judge whether the tenant will accept a termination fee, or take responsibility for the final lease.

Professional Sign-Off Required: commercial leasing counsel before the lease is signed.

The beginner mistake

Two opposite mistakes. The first is ignoring AI and paying a professional to do reading that a tool could organise in minutes. The second is treating the AI's output as the answer and acting on it without verification or sign-off. A confident, well-written paragraph is not evidence that it is true.

How you will use it

Use AI before and after professional advice, not instead of it. Before: to read, organise, find questions and draft your brief. After: to check that a final document matches what was agreed and to summarise it for your team.

Keep three rules. Do not paste confidential information into a tool without checking its terms. Verify any law or case it names before you rely on it. And keep the decision and the signature with a person who can be held responsible.
checklist: Sort the task: reading and organising, or judgment and responsibility.
Use AI to list dates, payments, consents and differences from your standard.
Ask AI to argue against your position.
Check the tool's terms before pasting confidential material.
Verify every rule or case the AI names.
Keep the decision and the signature with a responsible person.
Send your professional a short, organised brief, not a pile of documents.

selftest.q: Your site manager uses an AI tool to answer the question "Can we start excavation before the permit is issued?" and it replies "Yes, preliminary site work is generally allowed." What do you do?
selftest.a: Treat the reply as an unverified assumption, not an answer. The tool cannot know your municipality's current rules, the conditions on your development approval, or what your lender's documents require. Use the reply only to frame the question: what is "preliminary work" in this municipality, which rule decides it, and who must confirm it. Get written confirmation from the permitting authority or your planning professional before any excavation. Starting work without a required permit can be costly and hard to undo. Professional Sign-Off Required: planning professional and, if in doubt, municipal counsel.

apply: Take one contract you need to review this month. Ask an AI tool to list its dates, payments, consent requirements and termination rights in a table. Check three items against the original document yourself. Note anything it got wrong.

The university was reported to be considering an appeal. Read the decision itself before quoting its reasoning. His views come from the At The Top podcast episode "AI is already better at lawyering than humans" (https://youtu.be/mrBWJYkDNkI); the course author worked from the episode description, not a transcript. Baker's statements about AI's abilities are his opinions and are taught as such. The point about privilege is a general concept and is tagged for confirmation. All figures are hypothetical. Education only.

title: Verify before asserting: primary sources and hallucination traps
summary: AI tools can produce legal rules and cases that sound right but are wrong, out of date or invented. This lesson teaches a short verification routine based on primary sources, so nothing you rely on or file rests on an unchecked claim.
body:
Bottom line. Never rely on a legal rule or a case because an AI tool named it. Find the primary source, read the exact words, confirm it is current and from the right jurisdiction, and only then use it. If you cannot verify it, label it unverified or leave it out.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, an AI tool writes by predicting what words are likely to come next. Most of the time that produces useful text. But it can also produce a case name, a section number or a quotation that looks completely real and does not exist. This is called a hallucination: confident output that is false.

This has already caused real harm. In a widely reported 2023 case in a United States federal court, Mata v. Avianca, lawyers filed a brief that cited court decisions invented by an AI tool, and the court sanctioned them. As reported in 2026, Australia's Fair Work Commission ordered a worker to pay 1,230 dollars in costs after relying on AI advice that the Commission described as plain wrong. And as reported, from 20 October 2026 the Commission requires a party to disclose when generative AI prepared a filing.

The lesson is simple. The tool is not the source. A source is the document the law actually comes from.

The framework

First, know the two kinds of source. A primary source is the law itself: the statute, the regulation, the court decision, or the signed contract. A secondary source is a description of the law: an article, a textbook, a website summary or an AI answer. Secondary sources help you find primary ones. Only primary sources prove what the law says.

  1. Find it. Locate the primary source in an official or reliable database. For statutes, use the government's official publication. For cases, use a recognised case law database or the court's own site.
  2. Read the exact words. Read the section or the passage itself, not a summary. Check that it actually says what the AI claimed.
  3. Check it is current. Statutes are amended. Cases are overturned on appeal. Confirm you are reading the version in force on the date that matters.
  4. Check the jurisdiction. A rule from Ontario does not decide a question in Alberta. A United States case does not decide a Canadian question.
  5. Check the fit. Ask whether the facts of the case or the scope of the section actually match your situation.
  6. Record it. Write the full citation, the date you checked, and where you found it.
  7. Disclose where required. Some courts and tribunals now require you to say when AI helped prepare a document. Check the rules of any body you file with.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer asks an AI tool whether a company can deduct interest on money it borrows to buy shares of another company. The tool answers confidently, names a section of a tax statute, and names two court cases with years.

The developer runs the routine. The statute section exists and deals with interest deductibility, but the tool's summary left out a condition about the purpose of the borrowing. One of the two cases exists and is relevant. The other cannot be found in any case database under that name or year. It was invented.

The cost of not checking is easy to picture. Suppose the company relied on the summary to claim interest of 60,000 a year that turned out not to be deductible. Over three years that is 180,000 of deductions denied, plus interest and possible penalties. A one-hour check costs far less.

Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor before any filing position is taken.

The beginner mistake

Checking that a source exists and stopping there. A real section with a wrong summary is just as dangerous as a fake case. The second mistake is assuming that a detailed answer, with section numbers and years, is more likely to be correct. Detail is easy to generate. It is not evidence. A third mistake is asking the same tool to confirm its own answer. A tool asked "is that case real?" may simply agree with itself. Only the database can confirm it.

How you will use it

Adopt one house rule for your companies: no statute, rate, case or deadline goes into a decision memo, a letter or a filing unless someone has read the primary source and recorded the citation and the date. Anything not checked is tagged "unverified, confirm independently".

When you use AI for research, ask it for the primary source, then go and read that source yourself. When your professional gives advice, you can ask, politely, which section or case it rests on. Good professionals welcome the question.

Keep the record of what you checked. A simple log with three columns, the claim, the primary source and the date checked, takes seconds to fill in. It protects you twice. It stops an unchecked claim reaching a decision, and if anyone later asks why you relied on something, you can show exactly what you read and when.
checklist: Ask for the primary source, not just the answer.
Find the source in an official or recognised database.
Read the exact words of the section or passage.
Confirm the version in force on the relevant date.
Confirm the jurisdiction matches.
Record the citation, where you found it and the date checked.
Check whether the court or tribunal requires AI disclosure.

selftest.q: An AI tool tells you that in your province a landlord can always keep a tenant's deposit if the tenant leaves early, and it names a section of a residential tenancy statute. Your property is commercial. What is wrong, and what do you do?
selftest.a: Two problems before you even check the section. First, jurisdiction and scope: a residential tenancy statute usually does not govern a commercial lease, so the rule may not apply at all. Second, the word "always" is a warning sign, because legal rules usually have conditions and exceptions. Steps: read the lease's own deposit clause, which is the primary source for a commercial deal; then confirm with counsel what statute, if any, applies to commercial leases in that province; and do not repeat the AI's claim to the tenant. Professional Sign-Off Required: commercial leasing counsel.

apply: Take one legal or tax statement you have relied on recently. Find its primary source, read the exact words, and write down the full citation, where you found it and today's date. If you cannot find it, mark it unverified.
sources: Mata v. Avianca, Inc. is a 2023 decision of the United States District Court for the Southern District of New York in which lawyers were sanctioned for filing AI-invented citations; it is widely reported, and the docket details should be confirmed independently before citing. The 1,230 dollar costs order and the Fair Work Commission disclosure requirement from 20 October 2026 are as reported in 2026 Australian legal press [confirm independently against the Commission's own published rules]. title: Drafting with AI: rubric, red team, defect list
summary: Good AI-assisted drafting is a process, not a single request. You write the rubric first, let the tool draft, then make it attack its own draft and keep a list of defects to fix, with every version saved.
body:
Bottom line. Do not ask an AI tool for "a letter" and send what comes back. Write the rubric first, which is the list of what a good draft must achieve. Let the tool draft. Then make it attack the draft from the other side's point of view, list every defect, fix them, and save each version.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, on the podcast that introduced this course, Greg Baker says he ran his case like a software project. As reported, he kept his documents in a Git repository, which is a tool programmers use to save every version of a file and see exactly what changed. He treated the final bundle of documents like a build, assembled the same way each time. And he says he anticipated the other side's arguments and drafted his replies before the hearing.

You do not need Git to use the idea. The idea is that a good draft comes from a repeatable process with checks built in, not from one inspired attempt. Lawyers do this by habit. They know what the document must achieve, they write, they review as if they were the opponent, and they fix.

The framework

  1. Write the rubric. A rubric is a short scoring list. Before any drafting, write what the document must do. For example: state the facts with dates; cite the exact clause relied on; make one clear request; set a deadline; avoid admitting anything; stay polite.
  2. Give the tool the inputs. Provide the relevant clauses, the timeline, and the rubric. Tell it what not to do, such as "do not invent facts; mark any gap as MISSING".
  3. Draft. Ask for a first draft that follows the rubric.
  4. Red team. A red team is a group, or in this case a role, whose job is to attack a plan to find its weaknesses. Ask the tool: "You are the other party's lawyer. List every weakness in this letter and how you would respond."
  5. Make the defect list. Combine the red team points and your own review into a numbered list: factual errors, missing evidence, weak arguments, risky wording, tone problems.
  6. Revise and version. Fix each defect. Save the new version with a number and a date. Never overwrite the old one, so you can always see what changed and why.
  7. Verify and sign off. Check every fact and clause reference against the source documents, then have a professional review anything with legal effect.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A contractor is 45 days behind on a building with a 2,500,000 contract. The contract allows liquidated damages of 1,000 per day and requires written notice of default.

The developer writes a rubric: cite the completion date clause and the notice clause; state the delay in days; reserve the right to claim 45,000 to date; request a recovery schedule within 7 days; admit nothing about design changes. The AI produces a clean draft.

The red team step finds three defects. First, the contractor will argue the developer's own design change in month two caused 20 days of delay, and the draft is silent on it. Second, the draft sends the notice to the project manager's email, but the notices clause requires delivery to a named officer at the registered address. Third, the draft says "we will terminate", which could commit the developer to a step it may not want.

Version 2 addresses the design change with the dates of approval, sends the notice the way the contract requires, and replaces "will terminate" with "reserve all rights under the contract". The developer's lawyer reviews version 2 in half an hour.

Professional Sign-Off Required: construction counsel before the notice is sent.

The beginner mistake

Skipping the rubric and the red team. Without a rubric, you cannot judge whether the draft is good, only whether it sounds good. Without the red team step, the first person to find the weakness is the other side. A third mistake is losing track of versions and sending the wrong one.

How you will use it

Set up a simple folder for every dispute or negotiation: one folder for source documents, one for drafts with numbered versions, and one text file for the defect list. That is your version of Baker's repository.

Keep a standard rubric for your common documents: default notices, consent requests, lender updates and responses to claims. Reuse it every time. Over a year, your rubric becomes a record of every mistake you have learned not to repeat, and your lawyer's review time falls because the drafts arrive cleaner.

One more habit is worth building. Before any meeting, mediation or hearing, run the red team step on your whole position, not only on a letter. Ask the tool for the three strongest arguments against you and draft a short written reply to each. As reported, this is what Baker did before his hearing. Walking into a room with your replies already written is very different from hearing the other side's best point for the first time.
checklist: Write the rubric before drafting.
Give the tool the source clauses and timeline, and tell it to mark gaps as MISSING.
Ask for a draft that follows the rubric.
Ask the tool to attack the draft as the other side's lawyer.
Make a numbered defect list and fix each item.
Save every version with a number and date.
Verify facts and clause references, then get professional review.

selftest.q: You use AI to draft a reply to a buyer who says your company breached a sale contract. The draft is well written and denies everything. What steps are missing before you send it?
selftest.a: The rubric and the red team are missing. First, write what the reply must achieve, for example: respond to each allegation, cite the relevant clauses, admit nothing unnecessary, and preserve your rights. Second, ask the tool to act as the buyer's lawyer and list the weaknesses; a blanket denial may conflict with documents the buyer already holds. Third, build a defect list, check every fact and clause reference against the contract and emails, and save numbered versions. Finally, because the reply may be used later as evidence, have counsel review it. Professional Sign-Off Required: commercial litigation counsel.

apply: Write a five-line rubric for the type of letter you send most often in your business, such as a default notice or a consent request. Save it where you will find it next time you draft one.

title: The brief to counsel: arrive prepared, cut fees
summary: Professional time is best spent on judgment, not on finding out what your question is. This lesson shows you how to write a one-page brief to your lawyer or accountant that cuts fees and improves the advice, while the responsibility stays where it belongs.
body:
Bottom line. Pay your lawyer for judgment, not for sorting your papers. Arrive with a one-page brief that states the goal, the facts with sources, the documents, the specific questions and the deadline. The meeting gets shorter, the advice gets sharper, and the responsibility for the advice stays with the professional who signs it.

In plain English

Mr Shabazz, most professional bills are driven by time. A large part of that time, especially early in a file, goes on working out what the client actually wants, collecting documents and building a timeline. That work is necessary, but much of it you can do yourself, better and faster, because you know the facts.

Greg Baker, whose self-represented win at Australia's Fair Work Commission introduced this course, makes the point on the podcast that arriving prepared lets a professional spend time on judgment rather than research. He also notes, in substance, that responsibility is the one thing AI cannot carry. The professional who signs still answers for the advice. Your brief should make their job easier without trying to take over that responsibility.

A brief here means a short written summary you give your professional before the meeting. It is not a legal document. It is a map. It tells the professional where you are, where you want to go, and which roads you have already checked.

The framework

A good brief fits on one page and has seven parts.

  1. Goal. One sentence on the business outcome you want. "Transfer the lot into the operating company this year at the lowest lawful cost."
  2. Decision needed. What you must decide, and by when. "Whether to sign the transfer before the lender's renewal on 30 June."
  3. Facts, with sources. Short numbered facts, each with the document that proves it and its date. Mark anything unconfirmed as an assumption.
  4. Documents. A list of the attached documents, named and dated, in a logical order. Do not attach everything; attach what the facts rely on.
  5. Specific questions. Three to five precise questions. "Does clause 7.2 of the mortgage require the bank's consent to a transfer to a related company?" is better than "What should I do?"
  6. What you have already done. Searches run, people contacted, and any AI research, clearly labelled as unverified.
  7. Constraints. Budget, deadline, and anything you will not do.

Two rules apply. Be honest about bad facts; a lawyer who is surprised later costs more. And do not ask the professional to confirm your AI research line by line; ask your real questions and let them choose how to answer.

A worked example

Hypothetical. A developer needs advice on bringing a new investor into a company. In the first approach, the developer emails 40 documents with a note saying "please review and advise". The lawyer, at 500 per hour, spends six hours reading, building a timeline and sending follow-up questions, which is 3,000 before any advice is given.

In the second approach, the developer sends a one-page brief. The goal is to issue 20 percent of the shares to the investor for 200,000. The facts list the current shareholders, the share classes and the existing shareholder agreement, with dates. Five documents are attached. Four questions ask whether existing shareholders have a right to buy new shares first, which approvals are needed, whether the shareholder agreement must be amended, and what the investor's minority protections should be.

The lawyer spends an hour and a half reading and an hour advising, about 1,250. The advice is better because the time went on the questions that mattered.

Professional Sign-Off Required: corporate counsel before any shares are issued.

The beginner mistake

Sending everything and asking "what do you think?". That transfers the sorting work to the most expensive person in the room. The opposite mistake is sending a brief that hides inconvenient facts or presents AI research as settled. The professional's advice can only be as good as the facts in front of them.

How you will use it

Make the one-page brief your standard before every lawyer, accountant or tax meeting. Use AI to help assemble it: to build the timeline, list the documents and sharpen the questions. Then check every fact against its source yourself.

Keep the brief and the professional's written answer together in the file. Over time you build a record of what was asked, what was advised and when. That record is valuable at the next deal, the next financing and the next dispute.

Finally, read the advice you receive with the same care you put into the brief. Check that each of your questions was answered. If one was not, ask again in writing. If the advice depends on an assumption, such as a valuation or a date, make sure that assumption is true before you act. The professional carries responsibility for the advice. You carry responsibility for giving them accurate facts and for acting within the limits of what they said.
checklist: State the goal in one sentence.
State the decision needed and its deadline.
List numbered facts, each with a source and date.
Attach only the documents the facts rely on, named and dated.
Ask three to five precise questions.
Disclose what you have already done, labelling AI research as unverified.
State your budget and constraints.

selftest.q: You want your accountant's advice on paying yourself from your company this year. Write the specific questions section of a brief, with three questions.
selftest.a: Example questions: (1) Given my expected personal income and the company's expected profit this year, what mix of salary and dividends do you recommend, and what does each option cost in total tax across me and the company? (2) Are there any amounts I have taken from the company this year that should be treated as a shareholder loan, and what must happen to them by year end? (3) What filings and deadlines does your recommendation create for the company and for me? Each question is specific, tied to a decision, and leaves the professional judgment to the accountant. Professional Sign-Off Required: tax advisor.

apply: Choose the next professional meeting on your calendar. Write a one-page brief using the seven parts, and send it to the professional at least two days before the meeting.
